query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post-solidification heat treatment that induces nanoscale precipitate formation specifically at the lamellar colony internal boundaries will enhance the interfacial cohesion to both blunt microcrack initiation and impede crack propagation, thereby simultaneously increasing strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit numerous internal boundaries prone to microcracking under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized annealing treatment designed to precipitate nanoscale secondary phases selectively at the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: The annealing must be carried out under a temperature–time regime that promotes nanoscale precipitation without inducing coarsening of the primary lamellar phases or the onset of embrittlement, maintaining similar overall phase fractions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale precipitates localized along the internal colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates act as interfacial reinforcements that pin the boundaries, reducing the effective stress concentration and blunting crack tips. This dual role—providing local strengthening and limiting crack propagation—helps enhance yield strength while delaying catastrophic failure, thereby improving overall ductility relative to the untreated microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit increased yield and ultimate strength along with higher tensile ductility in room-temperature tensile tests, with microstructural analysis showing an abundance of nanoscale precipitates at the colony boundaries.
generation.baseline: The unmodified lamellar-colony microstructure obtained via conventional processing, which shows room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only in eutectic high-entropy alloys with similar dual-phase lamellar microstructures and within a specific annealing temperature/time window that avoids unwanted coarsening or secondary phase embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The kinetics of nanoscale precipitate formation in the dual-phase lamellar colonies and their stability under subsequent mechanical loading are not well-established; potential risks include the formation of overly coarse or continuous interfacial phases that might instead embrittle the alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set processed using conventional methods (baseline) and another set subjected to the optimized heat treatment intended to promote nanoscale precipitation at the lamellar boundaries. Perform detailed microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM, SEM) to document precipitate formation and distribution, and conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves to extract yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure.
Microscopy (TEM/SEM) images confirming the presence, size, and distribution of nanoscale precipitates at the internal boundaries.
Fractography to assess crack initiation and propagation characteristics.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in both strength and ductility over the baseline, or if the intended nanoscale precipitates are not observed at the lamellar boundaries, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high-entropy alloys established the promise of dual-phase lamellar colonies for high strength and acceptable ductility (PMC4145285). Later studies refined the lamellar architecture through thermomechanical processing (e.g., ultrafine grain refinement in PMC6353877 and the creation of dual heterogeneous microstructures in PMC6687781) to further enhance the strength–ductility synergy. These works progressively inherited and modified the as-cast lamellar microstructure; however, while they improved overall mechanical responses, the intrinsic propensity for microcrack initiation at the many internal interfaces has not been fully conquered.
decision.unsolved: The persistent issue is that the internal boundaries in dual-phase lamellar colonies act as sites for microcrack nucleation under room-temperature tensile deformation. Although processing routes (including grain refinement and dual heterogeneity) improve work hardening and limit crack propagation to some extent, they do not sufficiently tailor the interfacial characteristics to simultaneously boost strength and ductility. The boundary conditions of the current lamellar framework still host incoherent or weak interfaces that concentrate stress.
decision.lever: engineering interfacial chemistry/coherency via controlled thermal treatments that promote targeted solute segregation at phase boundaries
decision.why: Building on the trend where microstructural modifications improved the composite behavior without fundamentally altering the weak, numerous internal interfaces, the next logical step is to directly modify these boundaries. By inducing a deliberate solute segregation (or formation of a nanoscale interphase) at the lamellar interfaces, one can enhance interfacial coherency and reduce stress concentrations that trigger microcracking. This approach is testable via heat treatments (or low-temperature annealing) designed to produce graded composition profiles at the interfaces, with expected outcomes of increased tensile strength and ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline. Prior evidence in related HEA and refractory alloy systems (where coherent nanoprecipitates and interfacial tailoring improved ductility without sacrificing strength) supports this hypothesis.
